cells.tense: You are tending something that keeps other people moving, and you are doing it from feeling rather than force.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you're keeping going, and what you'd set down tomorrow if nothing else needed it.
cells.core: You keep a fire going that other people warm themselves by. They come to you when their own drive runs thin, and you hand them some of yours without making a show of it. What makes it work is that you're not forcing it — you actually feel the thing, and that feeling is what people catch. So you adjust as the room changes. Someone's low, so you give more; someone's stepping up, so you step back. That adjustment happens in you before you've decided anything. The good version looks like momentum that outlasts you, something still moving when you've left the room, because you built conditions rather than dependencies. There is more in you than this. The invitation isn't to tend harder. It's to notice what it's been feeding, and let some of that come back to you.
cells.sheetLine: You keep other people's momentum going, and you do it from feeling.
cells.verb: Keeping a fire going that others warm themselves by
cells.place: The mixing desk, where levels get adjusted as the room changes

cells.tense: You are bracing against a moment that hasn't arrived, managing a fire nobody has asked you to hold yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding for someone else and tell them plainly you won't carry it this week.
cells.core: You are getting ahead of a moment that hasn't arrived. The fire is burning fine right now, and you're already reaching for the next log, the next spark, the next thing that might go out, managing a room that isn't even in trouble yet. What you're actually doing is keeping the whole thing aloft by yourself, because if you stop adjusting, it might fall, and then what. People feel the strain even when they can't name it. They stop bringing you their real state, because you've already decided what it needs to be. Your drive is real and it isn't the problem. The problem is you've made yourself the only one who gets to keep it going. Setting down one thing you're holding for someone who could carry it themselves isn't abandoning the fire. It's letting it be theirs to tend.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding a fire nobody asked you to keep.
cells.verb: Keeping a fire going that others warm themselves by
cells.place: The mixing desk, where levels get adjusted as the room changes

cells.tense: You stopped feeding the fire some time back, and you are in a room you used to keep warm.
cells.ask: Tell one person the thing you've been not-doing, and ask them to check in on it with you next week.
cells.core: There's a fire you stopped feeding. Not because it went out, but because tending it started costing something you weren't willing to keep paying, so you set the log down and took a few steps away from it. You know where everything is in that room. You just don't reach for it anymore, and you've been calling that being realistic. The drive is still there. What you're not doing is picking anything up, and the longer you keep that distance, the more the room starts to feel like it belongs to someone else. Something in your life did need to end. You're not wrong about that. But you've treated the ending as the whole story, and it isn't. Endings clear ground. What you're on now is clear ground, and the next thing doesn't need the old fire back. It needs you to pick up one log and see what happens.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped feeding it, and the room still has your things in it.
cells.verb: Keeping a fire going that others warm themselves by
cells.place: The mixing desk, where levels get adjusted as the room changes

cells.tense: You are keeping a group's momentum alive in small adjustments you don't count as anything.
cells.ask: Name one adjustment you made this week to keep someone going, and say out loud that you made it.
cells.core: You keep a group's momentum alive in small adjustments you don't count. Someone's flagging in a project, and you shift how you talk to them. A room's energy drops, and you say the thing that gets it back without anyone noticing you said it. A friend's fire is low, and you find the one question that relights it. It costs you attention regularly, and you've filed it under just being a decent person, or just doing your job, or nothing at all. Meanwhile you tell yourself the real work is somewhere else, the thing you haven't started yet, the bigger fire. So the fire you're actually keeping gets filed as no one's. When you notice yourself holding something up, say so. Not for praise. To know what you're doing.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending this fire. You just haven't counted it.
cells.verb: Keeping a fire going that others warm themselves by
cells.place: The mixing desk, where levels get adjusted as the room changes
